idiom_name: indirect enum tree + struct Loc with an array of frames
implementation_notes: Swift's closest analogue of a functional datatype is an indirect enum (the recursive case is boxed automatically), so the tree and the context can be value types and the location is a struct pairing the focused subtree with an array of frames holding the parent's children and the hole. What replaces the classic structure is value semantics plus copy-on-write arrays: rebuilding the path is cheap, earlier locations stay valid, and no parent pointers are needed; what stays hand-written is the context type, since neither the standard library nor Foundation provides a zipper. First-class Collection.Index cursors already cover flat sequences, so the zipper only pays off for genuinely tree-shaped data, and class-based nodes with weak parent references remain the mutable alternative.
pitfalls: indirect enum boxes every recursive case on the heap, so a large tree is one allocation per node - use a class or an arena representation for big or hot trees.
Copy-on-write protects only the standard containers: a class instance stored inside the value tree is shared and mutable, which silently breaks the version guarantee.
Recursive pattern matching over deeply nested enums is stack-bound and verbose; an iterative walk with an explicit stack is safer for unbounded depth.
Class-based parent references need weak to avoid retain cycles, and they reintroduce the reference semantics the zipper was chosen to avoid.
